They're different: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive only reuses one TCP connection, but requests on it still go one after another, which is why browsers open several connections in parallel. HTTP/2 multiplexing sends many requests at once as interleaved streams over a single connection and compresses headers, though TCP-level head-of-line blocking remains.

They're not the same: keep-alive only reuses the TCP connection, but on it requests still go one at a time, so a slow response blocks the ones behind it, which is why browsers open several connections per host. HTTP/2 multiplexing interleaves many request and response streams on a single connection at once, with header compression, so no extra connections are needed. HTTP/2 still has head-of-line blocking at the TCP level on packet loss, which HTTP/3 over QUIC addresses. `as const` changes the inferred type: literals stay literal and everything becomes readonly, but it checks nothing. `satisfies` checks the value against a type (so typos and missing keys error) without changing the inferred type, and `as const satisfies Config` gives you both.
Action: None, happy to show an example from our code if useful.

`as const` freezes a literal's type: properties become readonly and values become literal types (an array becomes a readonly tuple). `satisfies` checks that a value fits a type without changing the inferred type, so you get errors on mismatches but keep the narrow type (`const x = { a: 1 } satisfies Record<string, number>` still has `a: number`, not an index signature). They combine well: `{ ... } as const satisfies Config`. Action: if you have a concrete object you keep tripping over, paste it and I'll show which one you want.
